title: Imparfait or passé composé?
topic: choosing between imparfait and passé composé
why: Now that you know both past tenses, this lesson teaches you to choose between them: the imparfait for the scene, habits and actions in progress, the passé composé for events and interruptions. It's the central difficulty of the French past for English speakers, practiced with many examples in context.

{"lessons": ["

The scene and the action

This is the central difficulty of the French past for English speakers, because English often uses the same simple past for both (\"it rained\", \"I went out\"). Think of a film. The imparfait is the set: the weather, the place, what people were doing. The passé composé is the action: what happens, step by step, and moves the story forward.

imparfait: the scenepassé composé: the events
background, descriptionan action that happened, complete
an action in progress (\"was -ing\")an action that interrupts it
a habit (\"used to\", \"would\")one single occurrence
no clear beginning or enda precise moment or a defined period
Il pleuvait quand je suis sorti.It was raining when I went out.
Je dormais quand le téléphone a sonné.I was sleeping when the phone rang.
Il faisait beau, alors on a pique-niqué au parc.The weather was nice, so we had a picnic in the park.

The pattern \"action in progress + interruption\" is extremely common: the long action in the imparfait, the short one that cuts in, in the passé composé. You can also use être en train de in the imparfait to stress the action in progress:

J'étais en train de cuisiner quand Paul est arrivé.I was in the middle of cooking when Paul arrived.

A quick English test: if you can say \"was -ing\" or \"used to\", it's an imparfait. If it's a step in the story that answers \"and then what happened?\", it's a passé composé.

", "

Habit or one time?

The same verb can go either way, depending on whether it's a habit or a single event. Compare:

Le dimanche, on allait au marché.On Sundays, we used to go to the market. (every week)
Dimanche, on est allés au marché.On Sunday, we went to the market. (once, last Sunday)
D'habitude, je prenais le bus, mais ce jour-là, j'ai pris un taxi.Usually I took the bus, but that day I took a taxi.

Words that point the way

Often with the imparfaitOften with the passé composé
d'habitude, souvent, toujoursun jour, une fois
tous les jours, le lundihier, lundi dernier
autrefois, quand j'étais petittout à coup, soudain
pendant queà ce moment-là

Pendant que (while) introduces a background action, so it's followed by the imparfait: Pendant que je cuisinais, Paul a mis la table. Tout à coup and soudain (suddenly) announce an event: Tout à coup, j'ai entendu un bruit.

A defined period, even a long one, takes the passé composé when you see it as finished: J'ai habité trois ans à Lyon (and then I left). Without the limit, it's description: À cette époque, j'habitais à Lyon.

To ask what happened, learn this question as a fixed phrase: Qu'est-ce qui s'est passé ? = What happened?

", "

Verbs that change meaning

Some verbs change meaning from one tense to the other. The imparfait describes a state; the passé composé marks the moment when something started or happened.

Verbimparfaitpassé composé
connaîtreje connaissais Marie: I knew Mariej'ai connu Marie: I met Marie (for the first time)
savoirje savais la vérité: I knew the truthj'ai su la vérité: I found out the truth
devoirje devais partir: I was supposed to leavej'ai dû partir: I had to leave (and I did)
avoirj'avais un chien: I had a dogj'ai eu un chien: I got a dog
Je devais venir, mais j'ai eu un problème.I was supposed to come, but I had a problem.
J'ai connu mon mari à Lyon. À cette époque, je ne connaissais personne.I met my husband in Lyon. At the time, I didn't know anybody.

Putting it together

Il était onze heures du soir. Il pleuvait et je rentrais chez moi en voiture. Tout à coup, la voiture est tombée en panne. Je n'avais plus de batterie sur mon téléphone, alors j'ai attendu.It was eleven at night. It was raining and I was driving home. Suddenly, the car broke down. My phone battery was dead, so I waited.

Look at the rhythm: the first sentences set the scene (était, pleuvait, rentrais), then tout à coup launches the events (est tombée, ai attendu). In the middle, je n'avais plus de batterie goes back to description.

When in doubt, ask: if I stop the film at this moment, is this something that is going on (imparfait) or something that happens (passé composé)?
